strengths: Novel problem formulation: Semantic-level triggers represent a genuinely new threat surface compared to existing word/syntax-level backdoor attacks, with well-motivated insight that semantically equivalent prompts should activate the same backdoor

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests on multiple models (SD v1.5, SDXL), 6 baseline attacks, 4 defenses, with extensive ablations demonstrating 100% ASR and significant detection rate reductions (12-25.8% vs. 68-100% for baselines)

Solid theoretical foundation: Rigorous analysis of semantic generalization (Theorem B.3, Corollary B.4) and convergence proofs for distillation optimization with AMSGrad, providing formal justification for the approach

Strong stealthiness across heterogeneous defenses: Maintains consistent low detection rates (39.5-57%) compared to baselines that are effective against some defenses but not others, suggesting robust evasion strategy

Thoughtful component design: Semantic regularization with length-prioritized sampling effectively prevents partial activation; multi-entity targets increase attention diversity with empirical validation showing detection rate increase from single-entity baseline

Clear motivation and presentation: Effective figures and logical progression effectively communicate the core insight that triggers should operate in continuous semantic space rather than discrete textual space
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in execution: Core mechanism (cross-attention projection editing via distillation) directly builds on Wang et al. (2024a) and Li et al. (2024b); main innovation is conceptual rather than methodological

Semantic trigger construction underspecified: Paper lacks clear explanation of how 11 semantically equivalent trigger prompts are created; choice of semantic elements (subject/action/object/scene) appears ad-hoc without justification for sufficiency or generalizability to other backdoor types

Incomplete defense evaluation: Only evaluates input-level defenses; missing evaluation against model-level defenses (parameter inspection, gradient analysis) and lacks discussion of potential semantic-space-aware defenses, limiting assessment of actual threat severity

Unvalidated semantic stability assumptions: Assumption B.1 (semantic stability in encoder space) relies on empirical observation in Figure 2 but lacks analysis of how to set ε_sem in practice, sensitivity to assumption violations, or whether stability holds uniformly across semantic regions

Strong white-box threat model: Requires attacker to modify model parameters before deployment; practical applicability limited without addressing gray-box scenarios or explaining how to construct high-quality semantic paraphrases

Limited experimental scope: Only two model architectures, single dominant backdoor target type, evaluation on only 100 test prompts; lacks analysis of performance variation across diverse semantic triggers and backdoor scenarios

Missing failure mode analysis: No discussion of which semantic regions are difficult to trigger, sensitivity to semantic composition choices, or how semantic drift with model updates affects robustness

Reproducibility gaps: Code availability not mentioned, hyperparameter choices (αk, αv) lack justification, trigger prompt construction procedure not fully specified, hindering reproduction and application to new scenarios

Loose theoretical bounds: Convergence analysis produces bounds dependent on unknown constants C1, C2; practical utility limited, and empirical convergence rates not validated against theoretical predictions

Limited defense guidance: Impact statement and conclusion provide minimal actionable direction for defenders; paper serves as security alert but offers little guidance for developing robust countermeasures

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with strong empirical evidence for semantic clustering in T2I representation spaces
Comprehensive method design combining semantic triggers, regularization, and multi-entity targets with clear technical exposition
Strong experimental results: 100% ASR on both SD v1.5 and SDXL with good utility preservation and substantial reduction in defense detection rates (2-25.8%)
Theoretical support through Theorem B.3 on semantic generalization of projections and convergence analysis with reasonable assumptions
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple baselines, defenses, and ablation studies with robustness to fine-tuning
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core distillation-based editing approach directly builds on prior work (Wang et al. 2024a, Li et al. 2024b); primary contribution is problem formulation rather than methodology

Evaluation fundamentally limited by exclusive reliance on GPT-4-generated test prompts that likely cluster near training distribution; missing human paraphrases and adversarial semantic variations; '100% ASR' claim misleading as it only tests same semantic composition

Semantic-level claims undermined: method still operates on text-based trigger definitions through manually chosen CLIP embeddings; distinction from syntax-level attacks unclear; no demonstration of language-independence

Semantic regularization inadequacy: contiguous token substrings poorly proxy semantic completeness; cannot prevent activation when semantic elements present in different structural arrangements; generalization beyond seen substrings undemonstrated

Critical missing evaluations: (1) no false positive rate on benign prompts, (2) no robustness test when trigger semantics present but in different compositions, (3) no analysis of activation with partial semantic information

Multi-entity target design incompletely analyzed: 'semantically related' criterion vague; Table 2 comparison potentially unfair as baselines not similarly modified; mechanism for selecting entities not systematized
White-box threat model realistic concerns unaddressed: no discussion of backdoor verification before distribution, survival under quantization/pruning, or comparison with data-poisoning trade-offs
Hyperparameter justification weak: crucial values (αk, αv, λreg) chosen via Figure 9 without principled justification; sensitivity to these and optimizer settings unexplored
Reproducibility gaps: no code, manual paraphrase generation not reproducible, GPT-4 test prompts not provided; Assumption B.1 (bounded encoder stability) used but actual εsem values never measured

strengths: Novel semantic-level backdoor concept: First work to explore backdoors at the semantic representation level rather than discrete textual patterns, opening an important new threat vector
Well-motivated threat model with clear advantages: Operating in continuous semantic space provides resistance to enumeration-based input defenses and attention consistency detection
Technically sound approach: Distillation-based cross-attention editing with semantic regularization is elegant and well-designed; multi-entity targets are clever contribution for evasion
Rigorous theoretical grounding: Formal analysis in Appendices B and C proves projection-level alignment generalizes across semantic variations and provides convergence guarantees
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Testing on 2 models, 6 baselines, 4 state-of-the-art defenses with thorough ablations; achieves 100% ASR with high CLIPp and most stable defense performance
Robustness demonstration: Maintains ASR >90% against fine-tuning-based defenses, showing resilience to common countermeasures
Excellent presentation: Clear writing with effective visualizations (Figures 1-3, 6) that clearly convey technical concepts and motivate design choices
Responsible research practices: Acknowledges ethical implications, uses secure evaluation environment, commits to not releasing malicious artifacts
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Technical implementation primarily adapts existing model editing techniques to semantic space; core contribution is conceptual rather than algorithmic

Incomplete technical specifications: Trigger prompt construction methodology unclear; rationale for contiguous substring regularization underjustified; semantic component extraction procedure not detailed; no computational cost analysis provided

Narrow experimental scope: Only 2 model variants tested (both Stable Diffusion); test prompts generated by GPT-4 with unspecified methodology; no evaluation across diverse semantic domains or complexity levels

Restrictive threat model: Requires white-box weight access and model distribution pre-deployment; doesn't address detectability of weight modifications or model verification barriers in deployment pipelines

Theoretical gaps: Assumption B.1 (semantic stability) depends on CLIP behavior with unclear domain applicability; bounds depend on difficult-to-estimate parameters (B_Q, B_H, L_sm); local stability analysis doesn't characterize global trigger region properties

Insufficient defense discussion: Vague recommendations for counter-defenses beyond concluding that future work should 'reason about semantic representations'; minimal exploration of detection approaches via representation analysis or model interpretability

Reproducibility limitations: No code availability mentioned; missing GPT-4 prompting details for test set generation; unclear semantic role extraction methodology; insufficient details on CLIP preprocessing

Limited failure analysis: No systematic study of which semantic compositions are difficult to encode; unclear how performance degrades with semantic complexity; insufficient characterization of trigger region boundaries and controllability via λ_reg

strengths: Novel and important contribution: Introduces semantic-level backdoors as a previously underexplored vulnerability class in T2I diffusion models, moving beyond enumerable word/syntax-level attacks
Strong empirical results: Achieves 100% ASR while reducing SOTA defense detection rates to 2-25.8%, demonstrating substantial effectiveness across multiple defenses

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Thorough comparisons with 6 baseline attacks and 4 defenses, extensive ablation studies, multiple metrics, and stability analysis across random seeds on two major architectures

Theoretical support: Provides semantic generalization analysis (Theorem E.3, Corollary E.4) justifying representation-level alignment across surface forms, plus convergence analysis of optimization procedure

Well-designed method: Multi-entity targets effectively evade attention-consistency defenses; semantic regularization successfully controls trigger boundaries; practical threat model requiring no downstream training data

Quality presentation: Well-organized paper with effective visualizations (especially Figure 3), clear writing, and substantial supplementary material including detailed proofs and additional experiments
Responsible research practices: Explicit impact statement, commitment to not releasing artifacts, local evaluation environment
weaknesses: Limited generalization testing: Test prompts maintain high semantic similarity (0.65-0.94 CLIP similarity) to training triggers; generalization to truly novel semantics beyond local trigger region unclear; '100% ASR' claim potentially misleading regarding true semantic generalization

Manual construction requirements: Requires manually curating 11 semantically equivalent trigger prompts and multi-entity targets, significantly limiting reproducibility and practical applicability; no analysis of sensitivity to these design choices

Incomplete semantic regularization: Uses contiguous token substrings which may not capture all partial semantic combinations; Table 2 shows non-zero FTR for 'Semantic Adjacent' (6.2% SDv1.5), indicating trigger boundaries aren't perfectly bounded

Limited defense exploration: Focuses on input-level defenses; model-level defense evaluation minimal (Section 5.6); no semantic-aware defenses tested; crucially, paper proposes attack without offering defensive solutions or mitigations

Experimental concerns: FID scores suspiciously identical between benign/backdoored models (~23.8-24.5); CLIPp metric measures semantic alignment not perceptual quality; comparison with IBA somewhat unfair (different target layer)

Theoretical limitations: Convergence rate O(1/√T) is standard; bounds contain potentially large multiplicative factors; assumes local boundedness/Lipschitzness without characterizing when these hold; gap between theory (AMSGrad) and practice (Adam)

Limited architectural scope: Only Stable Diffusion variants tested; unclear if approach generalizes to other T2I architectures or semantic decomposition schemes; no analysis of applicability to attention-free diffusion models
Reproducibility issues: Code not provided at review stage; CLIP encoder version unspecified; no sensitivity analysis beyond Figure 9; implicit assumptions about monitoring during injection phase

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Introduces semantic-level backdoor attacks operating in continuous representation space, a previously underexplored threat for T2I models with clear motivation against enumerable discrete triggers

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Extensive evaluation on SD v1.5 and SDXL with multiple metrics (ASR, FTR, FID, CLIP), thorough ablations, stability analysis across trigger-target pairs and random seeds, and testing against four different defense methods

Strong empirical results: Achieves 100% attack success rate while reducing defense detection rates from high levels to 2-25.8%, demonstrating practical effectiveness against existing input-level defenses
Clear presentation and methodology: Well-designed figure (Figure 3) illustrating all four components; semantic trigger construction using paraphrases is intuitive and easy to follow
Theoretical grounding: Provides formal analysis of semantic generalization (Theorem E.3, Corollary E.4) and convergence properties (Theorem F.4), with proofs in appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core components are not new—paraphrasing for triggers, cross-attention editing, L2 distillation, and substring regularization are all straightforward applications of existing techniques. Main contribution is their combination rather than fundamental innovation

Weak theoretical contributions: Semantic generalization analysis (Appendix E) makes unjustified assumptions about CLIP encoder stability; bounds depend on undefined constants (C₁, C₂) with no practical relevance. Convergence analysis (Appendix F) is standard AMSGrad theory, disconnected from core narrative

One-sided defense evaluation: Compares only against input-level defenses the attack explicitly targets. Table 7 reveals defense accuracy on balanced test sets (48.5-57%) is only marginally above random (50%), contradicting claimed robustness. No evaluation against model-level, semantic-aware, or adaptive defenses

Semantic regularization inconsistencies: FTR varies dramatically across models (Table 2: Missing Subject 7% SDv1.5 vs. 37.8% SDXL) without explanation. Residual FTR of 3-17.8% is non-negligible. Substring sampling schedule lacks algorithmic clarity

Overstated claims about non-enumerability: Continuous semantic space doesn't prevent enumeration if triggers occupy bounded regions (Figure 6 shows this). CLIP embeddings have limited diversity; defenders could sample semantic space. Claim that triggers are not enumerable is misleading

Reproducibility concerns: GPT-5 dependency for generating evaluation prompts is problematic (not publicly available). Hyperparameter choices (αₖ=5×10⁻⁴, αᵥ=1×10⁻³) appear somewhat arbitrary. Manual construction of 11 paraphrases introduces subjectivity with unclear process

Limited scope and scalability: Evaluation restricted to simple semantic compositions (cat chasing butterfly). No discussion of failure modes or performance on complex/abstract semantics. Only two model architectures tested (SD v1.5, SDXL). No analysis of how method scales

Threat model limitations: White-box weight-poisoning assumption is strong and potentially unrealistic for real-world scenarios. No discussion of detection mechanisms for suspicious model modifications. Assumes attackers have direct access to projection matrices

Insufficient defense discussion: Concludes with vague mention of future 'semantic-aware' defenses without concrete proposals. Provides no guidance on how defenders should adapt or trade-offs between utility and security. Multi-entity design lacks mechanical justification—why is it fundamentally harder to detect distributed patterns?

Missing comparative evaluations: No comparison against simple mitigations (prompt noise, CLIP ensembles, perturbations). Limited analysis of why semantic-level is fundamentally superior beyond empirical superiority over word-level baselines. No evaluation on other T2I models or with adaptive defenses designed after understanding semantic triggers

strengths: Novel semantic-level trigger concept: Introduces previously unexplored vulnerability class by shifting from discrete textual patterns to continuous semantic representations, with strong empirical validation via Figure 2 showing semantic similarity preservation across representation spaces

Strong experimental results: Achieves 100% ASR while maintaining good utility preservation (CLIPc 25.32, FID 23.83 comparable to benign model), substantially reducing defense detection rates (DSR: 2-25.8% vs. 22-100% for baselines)

Thoughtful technical design: Semantic regularization reduces unintended activation (FTR from 77.78% to 3.04%), multi-entity targets evade attention-consistency detection, well-motivated combination addressing both effectiveness and stealthiness

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Thorough ablation studies across multiple dimensions (λ_reg, α_k, α_v, trigger count, multi-entity design), stability across seeds and trigger-target pairs, robustness against fine-tuning and pruning, multiple evaluation models (SD v1.5, SDXL)

Theoretical grounding: Provides semantic generalization bounds (Appendix E) and convergence analysis (Appendix F) supporting empirical observations, formalizing why projection-level alignment generalizes across surface forms

Excellent presentation: Clear writing with well-designed figures (Figures 1, 2, 3), comprehensive appendices with detailed implementations, responsible research practices (local experiments, no model release, impact statement)
weaknesses: Unvalidated theoretical assumptions: Assumptions E.1-E.2 for semantic stability and boundedness are stated but not empirically validated against real CLIP embeddings; bounds tightness in practice unknown; no analysis of how projection matrix norms grow during optimization

Limited defense evaluation: Only evaluates against input-level defenses; no evaluation against adaptive defenses specifically designed for semantic-level attacks or model-level detection; Table 7 shows defense accuracy >50% indicating defenders still distinguish SemBD reasonably well

Ad-hoc semantic regularization design: Use of contiguous token substrings lacks principled justification; length-prioritized sampling schedule unjustified; some FTR values remain concerning (e.g., Missing Scene 17.8% on SDv1.5), raising questions about trigger specificity

Limited evaluation scope: Only two SD variants tested; fixed (subject-action-object-scene) trigger structure with no robustness evaluation for diverse semantic compositions; COCO evaluation limited to 5,000 samples; generalization to other T2I architectures unclear

Threat model considerations: White-box access requirement is relatively strong; paper doesn't discuss post-hoc detectability of cross-attention layer modifications; practical deployment path to open-source platforms unclear given increased scrutiny on model modifications

Incomplete technical analysis: Sensitivity to CLIP encoder versions not addressed; CLIP similarity range (0.65-0.94) is loose without robustness analysis; no computational cost comparison with baselines; GPT-5 evaluation prompt generation risks semantic leakage to defenders
